messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette failed validation. Make ONLY the targeted changes listed below.

Previous vignette:
Priya Singh is a 25-year-old counselor who came to treatment months after being thrown to the ground and restrained by police outside a bus stop on her way home from work. She had stepped in when officers were shouting at a young man nearby, and when she raised her voice one officer turned on her, forced her face toward the dirt at the edge of the sidewalk, and pinned her there while another stood over her. What remains sharpest is not a tidy narrative but fragments that arrive with brutal force: the smell of damp soil inches from her nose, the pressure in her shoulders and arms, the sight of dark uniforms and hard, unreadable faces above her. At other times she can recount the incident in a flat, strangely detached way, as if she is describing something that happened to someone else. Because these fragments returned so vividly and without warning, she began to find pieces of them everywhere in ordinary life; after a reliving, she would move through the day newly caught by damp pavement, dark uniforms, or the angle of a stranger looming in her peripheral vision, as though the memory itself had taught her what to notice. But when the memory breaks through fully, it comes back across all her senses at once, and her body draws in on itself as if she is again held down in that same twisted position.

In the weeks afterward, everyday parts of city life became loaded. Riding the bus to her counseling job began to feel unbearable. The hiss of the doors, the packed aisle, and especially any glimpse of police near a transit stop could pull the scene back into the present with such force that she would cover her face with her hands and get off early. Even the smell of wet ground outside her apartment complex or near the clinic after rain could bring back the dirt at her mouth and cheek, and with it a wave of shame and the thought that she was still somehow unclean from what had happened. She had come to believe that something about the assault had marked her, contaminated her, and when these moments hit she became desperate to hide herself or scrub away the feeling.

Priya also found that the way she now understood people sharpened the danger in ordinary encounters. She was certain that people are not what they seem, especially anyone wearing authority on their body. Once she had come to see authority as inherently threatening and the city as capable of turning on her without warning, far more of her surroundings began to register as possible signs of danger; a certain stance, a raised voice, even footsteps quickening behind her could snag her attention and feel like the start of something she needed to brace for. A police cruiser parked near her bus route no longer registered as background; it seized her attention immediately. She scanned officers’ faces, then everyone else’s, searching for the first sign of menace, and often felt her body surge before she had even formed a thought. That constant watchfulness followed her into the night. She lay awake feeling she had to stay alert, as though sleep itself would leave her unprotected. In that state, the city seemed full of cues that could set her off, and the more she monitored for threat, the more quickly the smell of earth, the bus, or the presence of police ignited the memory again.

Her attempts to manage this gradually narrowed her life. She stopped taking the bus whenever she could and spent money on rides she could not really afford. At work she checked mirrors repeatedly in hallways and bathroom sinks, looking behind herself before entering rooms. If she passed police on the street or outside the courthouse near her clinic, she lowered her head and covered part of her face with her hand. Over time, these habits seemed to draw the outline of the assault across her days: every mirror became a checkpoint, every altered route a reminder, and the more she organized her commute and workday around hiding, checking, and detouring, the more the bus stops, courthouse block, and even hallway reflections stood out to her as charged places she could not stop noticing. She also withdrew from people she used to feel rooted among, declining invitations from friends in her South Asian community because seeing them stirred too much of who she had been before the incident. She felt cut off from her community and culture, as if the assault had pushed her outside something familiar and protective. The isolation that followed only confirmed her sense that she no longer belonged and could not trust others to see or understand what had happened.

The memories themselves fed that withdrawal. After a vivid reliving, when her body had locked into the same braced posture and she could smell the soil again, she became even less willing to be around people or to put herself in situations she could not control. And when she later told herself the story in that numb, emotionless way, the detachment frightened her too; it seemed to prove that something fundamental in her had changed. She took both the reliving and the numbness as evidence that the event had lodged inside her and left her damaged. That conclusion made her more guarded with strangers and more suspicious of faces, which in turn kept her body primed and her attention fixed on possible danger.

By the time she sought help, the pattern had begun to affect her work as a counselor. On days when she had to commute, she arrived already exhausted from scanning the bus and the street outside the clinic for police, and after sessions she lingered by mirrors, checking behind her before leaving. What finally brought her in was a recent morning after rain: the smell of wet soil near the bus stop hit her, she saw two officers across the street, and before she knew what she was doing she was covering her face and stepping back as if she were about to be forced down again. She was shaken not only by the intensity of the reaction, but by the conviction that her world had become permanently unsafe and that she was disappearing from the people and communities that once made her feel like herself. What she wants most is to move through her city without bracing for attack; what frightens her most is that if this continues, she will lose both her work and her place among others.

Issues to fix:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not clearly state in the same paragraph that Priya’s negative beliefs directly lead her to avoidance, checking, hiding, or other maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: Although negative beliefs appear alongside memory in places, no paragraph explicitly conveys that the trauma memory itself leads to or drives her negative appraisals.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not explicitly describe her sense of threat causing the trauma memory to return within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph clearly states that perceived threat leads Priya to notice or experience more triggers/reminders, rather than only that threat monitoring makes cues stand out.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explicitly show her avoidance, checking, or withdrawal leading to stronger negative beliefs within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."

---

Return ONLY patch blocks — do NOT return the full vignette.

For each REQUIRED EDGE MISSING — produce one INSERT_AFTER block.
Find a paragraph in the vignette that already mentions component A, and add a sentence
after it that shows A influencing B through natural clinical language.
<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
[copy 1–2 sentences from the vignette — the anchor after which to insert]
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
[one or two sentences that convey A influencing B, written as natural clinical prose]
<<<END>>>

Output ONLY these patch blocks. No prose, no explanation, no full vignette.

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Even the smell of wet ground outside her apartment complex or near the clinic after rain could bring back the dirt at her mouth and cheek, and with it a wave of shame and the thought that she was still somehow unclean from what had happened. She had come to believe that something about the assault had marked her, contaminated her, and when these moments hit she became desperate to hide herself or scrub away the feeling.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Because she understood herself that way, covering her face, leaving places abruptly, and trying to wash off the feeling did not seem excessive to Priya; they felt like the only sensible ways to manage a world in which she had been visibly marked and could be exposed again.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
The memories themselves fed that withdrawal. After a vivid reliving, when her body had locked into the same braced posture and she could smell the soil again, she became even less willing to be around people or to put herself in situations she could not control.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Each time the memory returned with that force, the thought that followed came quickly: if it could still take over her body so completely, then something in her must have been permanently damaged by the assault.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
She scanned officers’ faces, then everyone else’s, searching for the first sign of menace, and often felt her body surge before she had even formed a thought. That constant watchfulness followed her into the night.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
On nights when she felt most sure that danger was close, the memory was also hardest to hold off; lying tense in bed, she would suddenly be back at the curb with the smell of damp soil in her nose and the weight on her shoulders.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
A police cruiser parked near her bus route no longer registered as background; it seized her attention immediately. She scanned officers’ faces, then everyone else’s, searching for the first sign of menace, and often felt her body surge before she had even formed a thought.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Living at that pitch of alarm made the city feel crowded with warnings, so that damp pavement, footsteps behind her, or a stranger's posture near a bus stop were all more readily taken in as reminders of what had happened.
<<<END>>>

<<<INSERT_AFTER>>>
Over time, these habits seemed to draw the outline of the assault across her days: every mirror became a checkpoint, every altered route a reminder, and the more she organized her commute and workday around hiding, checking, and detouring, the more the bus stops, courthouse block, and even hallway reflections stood out to her as charged places she could not stop noticing.
<<<NEW_SENTENCE>>>
Needing all of this to get through an ordinary day felt like its own kind of proof to Priya that she was no longer safe in the world and could not cope without these precautions.
<<<END>>>
